Trying to Conceive

Trying for a baby while COVID-19 is circulating

Updated: November 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Wanting a baby and feeling uncertain about COVID-19 can happen at the same time. A useful decision brings together your own health, the care you can access and the support available to you. This guide explains how to prepare, what to do if illness occurs while trying, and when physical or emotional symptoms need help.

Deciding whether to start trying now

Choosing a time to try for a baby can feel difficult when infection news, work pressures and uncertainty compete with your hopes. COVID-19 remains one consideration, but a headline cannot decide whether starting now or waiting is right for you. Think about your health, reproductive history, access to care, support and wishes together. Neither a blanket instruction to wait until COVID-19 disappears nor a promise that infection carries no pregnancy risk is a useful personal plan.

A short pause may help you arrange treatment, recover from illness or put practical support in place. For someone else, an open-ended delay could conflict with age-related fertility concerns or an existing treatment plan. Discuss what a delay would actually achieve and agree when to review it. You do not need a perfectly calm life to ask for preconception advice, and seeking advice does not commit you to trying immediately.

Understanding the risk without assuming the worst

Pregnancy and the weeks after it increase the risk of severe COVID-19 compared with not being pregnant. Age and other health conditions can add to that risk. Infection during pregnancy has also been associated with preterm birth and stillbirth, and some evidence links it with pre-eclampsia. Many people recover without serious complications, but that is different from saying that pregnancy, the placenta or the baby cannot be affected.

Evidence about early miscarriage and birth defects is more reassuring than some frightening online claims suggest. MotherToBaby’s December 2024 review reports that the studies it assessed did not find an increased miscarriage risk or a clear pattern of birth defects from COVID-19. These findings do not guarantee an individual outcome or cancel concerns about later pregnancy complications and fetal growth. Discuss your own illness and history rather than applying an old risk estimate to every variant, vaccination status and stage of pregnancy.

Review previous pregnancies, conditions and medicines

Arrange a preconception discussion if you have a long-term condition, take regular medicines, have had a complicated pregnancy or have questions about your health. Bring the names and doses of prescribed medicines, over-the-counter products, supplements and any fertility treatment. Ask whether your condition is adequately managed, whether anything needs changing before conception, and who will coordinate care if you become pregnant.

Do not stop essential treatment because you are worried about either COVID-19 or pregnancy. A medicine change may require a supervised plan, and untreated illness can also matter. Include the health of a partner who will contribute sperm. If a previous experience of loss or difficult care affects your decision, ask for time to discuss it rather than assuming that the same outcome will happen again.

Check how you will obtain care

Service availability differs between places and changes over time. Ask your local practice or maternity service how to arrange preconception advice, how to book after a positive pregnancy test, which visits need to be in person and whom to contact outside normal hours. Check transport, costs, interpreting needs and whether someone can help with childcare or accompany you when allowed. These are practical questions to resolve, not evidence that every service is currently disrupted.

Once pregnant, do not simply skip recommended appointments or scans to avoid exposure. If you develop symptoms before a visit, call the service: it can decide whether to alter the time, use a remote consultation or arrange an appropriate in-person assessment. A telephone or video appointment can be useful, but it cannot replace every examination, blood test or scan. Urgent concerns need the urgent route, even when a routine appointment is delayed.

Vaccination is part of preparation, not the whole decision

Check your current local COVID-19 vaccine advice and discuss the product, eligibility and timing with a clinician or vaccination service. As checked in November 2026, ACOG recommends vaccination for people contemplating or trying for pregnancy, and Canadian public-health advice also recommends vaccination when planning pregnancy. The evidence reviewed by these bodies does not show that COVID-19 vaccination causes infertility. Recommendations and access rules can differ between countries and services.

ACOG does not require delaying pregnancy after a COVID-19 vaccine series or booster; Canada similarly advises no delay after an mRNA vaccine. This answers the vaccine-timing question, not every medical or practical reason someone might choose to wait. Do not postpone a useful discussion while waiting for an unspecified future vaccine. Tell the service about a recent infection, previous reactions and other vaccines, because advice for a particular product or a different vaccine may be different.

Reduce exposure in ways you can sustain

Use several realistic precautions rather than expecting one measure to remove all risk. Cleaner indoor air, a well-fitting mask when appropriate, and avoiding close contact with people who are ill can complement vaccination. Discuss situations that matter in your own life, such as a crowded workplace, caring for a vulnerable relative or frequent healthcare visits. Household members can share the responsibility for reducing exposure.

If you develop respiratory symptoms, stay away from others as far as practical and follow current local advice about testing, staying home and returning to activities. The CDC’s public advice uses overall improvement and resolution of fever, followed by additional precautions; healthcare settings may have separate rules. A public-health return-to-activity rule is not a fertility clearance test. Continue needed care by contacting the service for instructions.

Prepare food, drink and daily habits

Start with ordinary preparation: a varied diet, support to stop smoking, avoidance of recreational drugs, and no alcohol while trying for pregnancy. Ask for help if changing a habit is difficult. Discuss weight and nutritional needs without crash dieting or treating a body-size target as a moral test. Both partners can benefit from practical changes, and health support should remain accessible while those changes are underway.

Because pregnancy may begin before a test becomes positive, it is practical to become familiar with pregnancy food-safety advice now. Wash produce, store chilled food properly and follow local cooking advice. NHS pregnancy advice limits total caffeine to 200 mg a day; count coffee, tea, cola, energy drinks and other sources together. Avoid liver and liver products in pregnancy because of their high vitamin A content. A special “immune-boosting” diet cannot guarantee protection from infection or conception success.

Use supplements for the right purpose

Folic acid helps prevent neural tube defects; it is not a COVID-19 treatment. NHS advice is 400 micrograms daily while trying, ideally starting before conception, and through the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. Some people need a prescribed higher dose because of particular conditions, medicines or a personal or family history. Ask which dose applies to you instead of combining several prenatal products.

Vitamin D advice depends on local guidance and individual circumstances. For example, NHS pregnancy advice recommends 10 micrograms daily from October to March, with year-round use considered or advised for some people with limited sunlight exposure or darker skin. This is UK seasonal advice, not a worldwide schedule. Check labels and avoid pregnancy supplements containing retinol or cod liver oil. More is not necessarily better; bring all supplements to your medication review.

Keep movement manageable at home or outside

Choose activity you can maintain, such as walking, gentle dancing, gardening or an appropriate class. Short periods of movement can be useful when time, weather or access to facilities is limited. An online class is an option, not a requirement, and it should suit your health and experience. If you are inactive, start gradually rather than making an abrupt change to intense training.

Once pregnant, adapt activity to how you feel and to any clinical advice. NHS guidance encourages moderate activity and suggests being able to talk while exercising; stop if you feel unwell rather than pushing through exhaustion or overheating. Ask about individual restrictions if you have a condition, symptoms or are receiving fertility treatment. Exercise can support wellbeing, but it is not a way to cancel infection risk or guarantee a pregnancy.

If you become ill while trying to conceive

Trying does not mean that pregnancy has definitely occurred. Tell the clinician or pharmacist that pregnancy is possible and when your last period started, especially before a medicine is prescribed. Most home pregnancy tests can be used from the first missed period; if you do not know when it is due, NHS advice is to test at least 21 days after the last unprotected sex. An early negative may need repeating after a few days.

Seek prompt advice about suspected COVID-19 if you are pregnant or have risk factors for severe illness. Selected treatments must begin early (within about five to seven days, depending on the treatment) so do not wait for symptoms to become severe or for repeated pregnancy tests before contacting care. Treatment choice depends on pregnancy possibility, other medicines and health conditions. Do not borrow antivirals or stop regular medicines yourself; indicated treatment should not be withheld solely because someone is pregnant.

Revisit timing after illness or difficulty conceiving

If either partner is unwell, allow space for recovery and ask whether lingering symptoms, a prescribed treatment or a planned fertility procedure changes the timing of attempts. There is no single recovery interval this article can prescribe for everyone. Fever or illness can temporarily affect male reproductive measures, but a change does not establish permanent infertility. Tell a fertility clinic about recent infection so results and treatment plans can be interpreted in context.

Do not let repeated postponements replace an indicated fertility assessment. ASRM’s 2026 guidance uses age, time trying and known reproductive conditions to guide when to investigate, and recommends earlier assessment when a relevant problem is already known. Ask for individualized advice if periods are irregular, there is a known fertility concern or you are worried about age. Where applicable, both partners should be considered; anxiety is not a sufficient explanation for difficulty conceiving.

Make room for worry without blaming yourself

Concern about illness, money, healthcare or becoming a parent can coexist with wanting a baby. Identify which concern can be acted on now and which uncertainty cannot be eliminated. You might ask a trusted person to help with appointments, agree a manageable time for checking reliable news, or write down questions instead of repeatedly searching for reassurance. Rest, enjoyable activities and supportive conversation can make the decision less isolating.

The relationship between stress and fertility is not fully understood. ASRM cautions against assuming that reducing stress will itself produce a pregnancy, and telling someone simply to relax can increase blame. Coping strategies are valuable because your wellbeing matters. You do not have to earn fertility care by becoming calm, and a failure to conceive is not proof that you worried too much.

Know when emotional support should become professional care

Ask for help if anxiety, low mood or intrusive worries interfere with sleep, work, relationships or daily life, or if your usual ways of coping are no longer enough. A clinician can discuss talking therapies and, where appropriate, medicines. Remote support may be available, but ask what the service actually offers and how to reach help between appointments. New symptoms deserve attention even if you have never had a mental-health problem before.

If you have a current or past severe mental-health condition, NICE advises considering specialist preconception counselling, preferably with a perinatal mental-health service. Discuss relapse prevention, pregnancy plans and the benefits and risks of treatment before making changes. A mental-health crisis needs urgent assessment. If a life is at risk, serious self-injury or an overdose has occurred, or you cannot keep yourself or someone else safe, seek local emergency help immediately; the person in crisis should not drive themselves.

Symptoms that should not wait for the planning appointment

For suspected COVID-19, get emergency help for trouble breathing, persistent chest pain or pressure, new confusion, inability to wake or stay awake, or pale, grey or blue lips, nail beds or skin. These are independent warning signs; do not wait for several to occur. Contact a clinician promptly for other severe or concerning symptoms, worsening illness or failure to improve, particularly if you are pregnant or at higher risk.

Pregnancy bleeding needs urgent clinical advice even when light. Get emergency help if bleeding is heavy, or occurs with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness. Do not assume these symptoms are simply COVID-19 or postpone assessment while waiting for another home test. Use the local emergency service when necessary and arrange an ambulance or another driver rather than driving yourself when seriously unwell.

Agree a plan you can review

Before deciding, write down what is ready, what still needs arranging and what would change your choice. That might include a medication review, an available appointment, recovery from illness, vaccination advice, a trusted support person or a mental-health care plan. If you decide to wait, agree a review point and seek contraceptive advice if you do not want pregnancy meanwhile. If you decide to try, keep the same care and support contacts available.

After a positive pregnancy test, arrange antenatal care promptly and mention your health history, medicines and any recent COVID-19 illness. A plan should be flexible enough to respond to changing circumstances without treating every news update as a reason to start again. You deserve clear information and support whether you choose to try now, wait, or reconsider your plans.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask which health, medication or pregnancy-history issues need attention before trying, and what a delay would achieve in your own circumstances.

Confirm local vaccine advice, booking arrangements, remote and in-person care options, and urgent contacts. Tell the team promptly if illness or pregnancy changes the plan.

Arrange practical and emotional support, including specialist advice for a severe mental-health history. Set a review point rather than treating uncertainty as a reason to wait indefinitely.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you organize questions, medicines, appointment details and a timeline of symptoms or pregnancy tests for your care team. It cannot decide whether conception is safe for you, diagnose COVID-19 or pregnancy, choose a treatment, assess a mental-health crisis or replace urgent care. Do not delay contact while completing a record.

When to seek help

Seek emergency help for trouble breathing, persistent chest pain or pressure, new confusion, inability to wake or stay awake, or pale/grey/blue lips, nail beds or skin. Pregnancy bleeding that is heavy or accompanied by severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness also requires emergency care. These are alternative triggers; do not wait for all of them. Serious self-injury, overdose or inability to keep anyone safe requires immediate emergency help. Arrange another driver or an ambulance when emergency assessment is needed. Seek urgent clinical advice for pregnancy bleeding even if light, a mental-health crisis, worsening illness or other concerning symptoms; tell the clinician if pregnancy is possible.

Evidence notes updated: November 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Starting now or waiting is an individual decision that includes health, fertility timing, care access and support; neither zero-risk promises nor blanket postponement are appropriate.
  • Pregnancy increases the risk of severe COVID-19. Current vaccine advice can help reduce risk, and vaccination itself generally does not require delaying conception under the cited guidance.
  • Prepare with appropriate folic acid, food safety, medicine review and manageable activity. Supplements and exercise cannot guarantee protection or pregnancy.
  • If illness occurs, say that pregnancy is possible and seek time-sensitive care when indicated. A negative test taken too early is not a reason to ignore serious symptoms.
  • Emotional support is worthwhile without promising fertility benefits. Persistent distress and urgent physical or mental-health symptoms deserve care.

Frequently asked questions

Should I wait until COVID-19 has gone away before trying?

There is no single yes-or-no answer for everyone. Consider your health, age and reproductive history, current illness, access to care and practical and emotional support. Discuss what a delay would improve and when to review it. Avoid both indefinite waiting based only on alarming news and reassurance that infection has no pregnancy risks.

Do I need to delay conception after a COVID-19 vaccine?

ACOG says pregnancy need not be delayed after a COVID-19 vaccine series or booster; Canadian guidance gives the same reassurance after mRNA vaccination. Check current local eligibility and product-specific advice. This does not remove a separate reason to review your health, medicines or recent illness, and it is not a rule for every other vaccine.

How can I prepare if I am spending more time at home?

Keep ordinary preparation achievable: arrange medication and health reviews, take the recommended folic acid, eat varied food, avoid alcohol and smoking, and find manageable ways to move. Check pregnancy food safety and your local vitamin D advice. Ask for help with isolation, costs or access to appointments rather than relying on a special supplement or an intense exercise programme.

What if I catch COVID-19 while trying?

Tell the care team that pregnancy is possible, but do not assume it is confirmed. Test at the appropriate time and repeat an early negative if necessary. Seek prompt assessment if you are pregnant or at increased risk because treatments can be time-sensitive. Do not delay needed care while repeating a pregnancy test, and check medicines with the prescriber or pharmacist.

Does COVID-19 always harm a pregnancy or fertility?

No. Many pregnancies are unaffected by serious complications, and available evidence does not support a claim that every infection causes miscarriage or birth defects. Nonetheless, pregnancy raises the risk of severe COVID-19, and infection is associated with some adverse pregnancy outcomes. Temporary reproductive effects can follow illness. Individual assessment is more useful than either a guarantee of safety or an assumption of permanent harm.

Can worrying stop me from becoming pregnant?

The stress–fertility relationship is uncertain, and reducing stress is not a guaranteed fertility treatment. Support, rest, enjoyable activity and talking therapies can help your wellbeing. Persistent symptoms or difficulty conceiving deserve assessment in their own right; neither should be dismissed by telling you to relax.

Should I avoid clinics to reduce exposure?

Do not simply miss recommended care. Ask the service about current arrangements, remote options and which examinations or scans must be in person. Tell it before attending if you have respiratory symptoms. Have an urgent contact route as well as a routine appointment plan, and do not delay emergency assessment because of exposure worries.

When should I get urgent help?

Emergency COVID-19 warnings include breathing trouble, persistent chest pain or pressure, new confusion, inability to wake or stay awake, or pale/grey/blue lips, nail beds or skin. Any one is enough to seek emergency help. Pregnancy bleeding with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness, loss of consciousness or heavy bleeding also needs emergency care. Mental-health emergencies include serious self-injury, overdose or inability to keep anyone safe. Seek urgent advice for pregnancy bleeding even if light and for other severe or worsening symptoms; do not wait for a routine planning visit.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
